title: Evaluating Reading Comprehension Exercises Generated by LLMs: A Showcase of ChatGPT in Education Applications
venue: Proceedings of the 18th Workshop on Innovative Use of NLP for Building Educational Applications (BEA 2023)
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of generating high-quality, personalized reading comprehension materials for middle school English learners using large language models, especially ChatGPT. The authors argue that existing reading exercises are often outdated, repetitive, and difficult for teachers to customize, and they explore whether LLMs can help produce more engaging and suitable passages and multiple-choice questions.

The intervention is a reading exercise generation system built around ChatGPT. The system uses carefully designed prompts to generate reading passages in zero-shot and one-shot settings, as well as multiple-choice questions and answers for those passages. It also includes a toxicity filter before materials are released. As a baseline, the authors fine-tune GPT-2 with PPLM control on teacher-provided middle school reading datasets. Teachers can edit generated content through a graphical interface, making the system teacher-facing rather than student-facing in primary use.

The study context is Chinese middle schools, specifically Grade 7 to Grade 9 English reading instruction in Beijing. Evaluation combines automatic text metrics, human ratings from Chinese college students and native English speakers, and feedback interviews with three experienced middle school teachers who used the system for a week. The results suggest ChatGPT-generated passages are often judged as comparable to or better than human-written passages on readability, coherence, engagement, and suitability, while the generated multiple-choice questions are relevant but still weaker than human-written ones in distractor quality and variety. Teachers reported that the system could reduce time and cost while supporting personalized resource creation, but also noted the need for better question generation.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational LLM chatbot used to generate and adapt reading comprehension passages and multiple-choice questions from prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Implemented in a reading exercise generation system for Chinese middle school English learners to produce zero-shot and one-shot reading passages, generate multiple-choice questions and answers, and support teacher editing; also evaluated for passage and question quality and suitability in school use.

findings.finding_summary: In human evaluation 1, ChatGPT-generated reading passages were rated higher than human-written passages across readability, correctness, coherence, engagement, and overall quality by 9 Chinese college students and 364 native English speakers. Reported mean scores for Chinese students were 4.61 vs 4.52 in readability and 4.46 vs 4.18 overall quality; for native speakers, overall quality was 4.06 vs 3.89.
findings.measure: Human-rated passage quality across readability, correctness, coherence, engagement, and overall quality
findings.sample_size: n=9 Chinese student evaluators; n=364 native English speakers; 30 passages rated in this evaluation

findings.finding_summary: In pairwise comparison, evaluators preferred ChatGPT passages over human-written passages and judged them as more likely to be human-written than the true human passages. Relative quality scores were 0.87 for ChatGPT zero-shot and 0.80 for ChatGPT one-shot versus 0.13 and 0.20 for the human-written counterparts in the paired comparisons.
findings.measure: Pairwise relative quality judgments and model-generated-versus-human discrimination for reading passages
findings.sample_size: n=9 additional student evaluators; 10 human-written passages plus 30 generated passages in this evaluation

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT passages showed high topic coherence with the given prompts, scoring 0.97 in both zero-shot and one-shot conditions, compared with 0.40 for the fine-tuned GPT-2 + PPLM baseline. This indicates strong prompt-following and topic control for reading passage generation.
findings.measure: Topic coherence of generated passages relative to specified topics
findings.sample_size: n=9 student evaluators; 10 topic pairs in the pairwise evaluation

findings.finding_summary: Evaluators judged ChatGPT passages to be suitable for middle school English learners, with suitability scores of 0.77 in both zero-shot and one-shot settings, compared with 0.37 for the baseline and 0.53 for human-written passages in the comparison task. The authors conclude the materials were largely suitable for real educational use.
findings.measure: Suitability of generated passages for middle school English learners
findings.sample_size: n=9 student evaluators in the suitability comparison

findings.finding_summary: For generated multiple-choice questions, ChatGPT produced items that aligned well with passage content (match score 4.38/5), but scores were lower than human-written questions on usefulness (3.25 vs 3.93) and suitability (3.48 vs 3.92). Evaluators also found generated questions more obviously model-like (0.67 vs 0.27), suggesting the questions were useful but still in need of teacher selection and refinement.
findings.measure: Human-rated quality of generated multiple-choice reading questions (match, usefulness, suitability, and whether they appeared machine-generated)
findings.sample_size: n=multiple human evaluators; 10 textbook exercises compared with 20 generated question sets

quality_tier_rationale: This is a primary evaluation study with multiple human-judgment tasks, but it is not an RCT/QED and does not report causal effects or robust experimental classroom outcomes. The evidence is nevertheless useful because it includes implementation details and direct user feedback from teachers in a school-oriented setting.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports strong positive quality judgments for generated reading passages, but no effect sizes or student learning gains are reported. The impact appears promising for instructional material generation, though the evidence is limited to prototype and evaluation data rather than demonstrated classroom achievement effects.
